structure.title: Chapters 1–5 · Norland changes hands
structure.text: A dying man's request seems generous enough until his son and daughter-in-law discuss exactly what generosity requires. Within pages the Dashwood women have lost both their house and most of the assistance their half-brother once imagined giving. The sum shrinks while his good opinion of himself survives.

structure.title: Chapters 6–25 · Barton Cottage and its visitors
structure.text: In Devonshire the family acquires kind, intrusive neighbours. A young man carries Marianne home after a fall. Elinor's attachment proceeds with considerably less publicity. In both cases the people watching a courtship have to infer a promise from conduct which may stop just short of making one.

structure.title: Chapters 26–41 · A London visit
structure.text: On a visit to town Marianne expects the next letter, the next knock or the next party to settle a question she considers already answered. Elinor has been entrusted with information she cannot share. The sisters keep one another company while each lacks something indispensable to understanding the other's distress.

structure.title: Chapters 42–50 · The journey back
structure.text: Travel, illness and reports brought by other people force a slower reckoning with what happened in London. The young women must decide which parts of another person's explanation deserve belief and what a truthful explanation might still fail to excuse.

people.name: Elinor and Marianne Dashwood
people.text: Elinor attends to practical obligations even when miserable. Marianne thinks feeling deeply ought to involve showing it. Each sister's conduct looks quite different once we see what it costs the other to live beside it, particularly when both are suffering at once.

people.name: Willoughby and Colonel Brandon
people.text: Willoughby knows exactly the poetry and music Marianne loves. Brandon's quiet manner looks comparatively unpromising to a girl who prizes candour. The ability to produce the right quotation on a walk is a real pleasure and an uncertain guide to how someone treats an absent woman.

people.name: Edward Ferrars and Lucy Steele
people.role: Visitors tied by a private history
people.text: Edward's awkwardness invites Elinor to supply generous motives for his reserve. Lucy makes remarkable use of the conventions of confidential friendship. A person who has promised discretion can be obliged to hear rather more than she wanted to know.

context.title: What constitutes an engagement?
context.text: A young couple may ride out, exchange keepsakes or show marked preference in company. Their families have strong reasons to read those signs as serious intentions. Whether an explicit promise was ever made matters enormously if somebody suddenly chooses to read them differently.

notice.text: Listen to John Dashwood talk a gift down.
notice.why: Every reduction in the proposed allowance brings with it a new reason why the beneficiaries are better off. Austen lets husband and wife perform the entire conversion of self-interest into family duty in an apparently affectionate conversation.

passages.quote: if the sum were diminished one half

notice.text: Notice the work Elinor's composure performs.
notice.why: If one sister leaves the room in distress, the other may have to entertain the guest, answer the question or get them both home. What looks from outside like an absence of feeling can contain a great deal of unpaid work on somebody else's behalf.

opening: The Dashwood sisters lose their home, and their well-off relatives find excellent reasons not to help very much. Elinor tries to keep the family steady; Marianne regards restraint as a poor substitute for feeling deeply. Both encounter men whose attentions are easier to interpret hopefully than accurately. Austen makes the courtship funny without forgetting its financial consequences, following what can happen when a woman must discover someone's intentions through visits, silences, and rumours while having very little power to demand a straightforward answer.
